AUT.story:
In September 1995 Cardinal Hans Hermann Groër, the Archbishop of Vienna, stepped down after former pupils accused him of sexual abuse. In 1998 the Austrian bishops said they considered the allegations well founded. In 2010 abuse at the boarding school of Kremsmünster Abbey in Upper Austria became public, and in 2013 a court sentenced its former boarding director, to 12 years in prison for abusing 24 boys.

In spring 2010 the bishops set up the Independent Victims' Protection Commission, chaired by Waltraud Klasnic, to pay victims of church abuse. By 31 August 2021 payments had been approved in 2,550 cases, about €33 million in total.

Inquiries into homes run by cities and states followed. In 2013 a commission on the city's Wilhelminenberg home found that girls as young as about six had been raped and sexually exploited there by caregivers and outside men, and that city staff and politicians who knew of it in the 1960s did not act. From 2010 the city paid the victim-support organisation Weisser Ring to handle claims, and by 2019 it had paid 42.13 million euros to victims. In 2015 a University of Innsbruck study for the states of Tyrol and Vorarlberg found that their homes kept children isolated and dependent on staff, a system that produced and tolerated sexualised violence until the 1980s.

In October 2025, after reporting by the magazine Falter, the Austrian branch of the SOS Children's Villages charity said there were credible allegations that its founder, Hermann Gmeiner, who died in 1986, had abused eight boys between the 1950s and 1980s. Victims had come forward from 2013 and been compensated, but the charity had not made this public. Prosecutors in three cities opened investigations, and in 2026 a reform commission chaired by the former Supreme Court president Irmgard Griss examined the lack of outside oversight of the villages.

Most of the abuse found in Austria took place in church, city and state homes between 1945 and the 1990s, and has mainly led to compensation payments. The allegations against Gmeiner, kept inside the charity for years, are still under investigation.

BRA.story:
In 2003 Brazil's Congress set up a CPMI, a joint inquiry of senators and deputies, to investigate networks that sexually exploited children and adolescents. Its final report in July 2004 named more than 250 people, among them 20 serving politicians, including three mayors, about 30 businessmen and five priests, and passed their cases to prosecutors. Its draft rewrite of the Penal Code chapter on sexual crimes became law in 2009.

From 2008 to 2010 a Senate inquiry chaired by Senator Magno Malta examined abuse material shared online. It reached an agreement with Google, the Federal Police and prosecutors to open the records of pages on the Orkut social network linked to child abuse. Laws passed during its work made possessing abuse material a crime. A Pará state deputy, Luiz Afonso Sefer, whose fall Malta credited to the inquiry, was convicted in 2010 of raping a child; the case has since been overturned, reinstated and annulled on appeal, and as of February 2026 his 20-year sentence had not been carried out. In 2014 a Chamber of Deputies inquiry asked for 37 people to be indicted, among them Adail Pinheiro, the mayor of Coari in Amazonas, and a serving state deputy.

Much of the exploitation takes place along roads and in tourist towns. The Federal Highway Police's 2021–2022 survey of more than 9,700 truck stops, bars and motels rated 640 of them critical. The 2025 US State Department trafficking report says taxi drivers and hotel, bar and nightclub staff in northeastern coastal resorts help foreign offenders reach children, and that no investigations of complicit officials were reported.

Brazil has the largest Catholic population in the world, but no national inquiry into abuse in churches or children's institutions has been found. Cases have come out one at a time, as in Arapiraca in 2011, when a judge convicted three priests of abusing altar boys.

Three congressional inquiries named politicians and led to new laws, and the conviction of at least one of those politicians has still not been enforced. Abuse inside Brazil's institutions has never been counted nationally.

CHN.story:
China opened intercountry adoption, the adoption of its children by families abroad, in 1992. About 160,000 children were sent abroad, many to the United States, which issued 7,906 visas to children adopted from China in 2005 alone. Between 2002 and 2005 six state orphanages in Hunan province bought infants from traffickers who brought them from Guangdong and placed nearly 1,000 of them with families in China and abroad. In 2005 the authorities fired 23 officials, and three traffickers were sentenced to 15 years in prison. According to the New Yorker, the programme came to depend more and more on abuse, abduction and trafficking. On 5 September 2024 China's foreign ministry announced its end, except for adoption by blood relatives or of a stepchild.

Trafficking also runs in the other direction, bringing women and girls from neighbouring countries to be sold to Chinese men and families as brides. In 2019 Human Rights Watch documented women and girls from Kachin and northern Shan states in Myanmar, many displaced by war, who were sold to Chinese families for US$3,000 to 13,000, locked up and raped so they would become pregnant. In Pakistan, the Federal Investigation Agency listed 629 girls and women sold as brides to Chinese men from 2018 to mid-2019. Officials told the Associated Press that the investigation largely stopped after June 2019 because government officials feared harming relations with Beijing, and in October 2019 a court in Faisalabad acquitted 31 Chinese nationals after witnesses were threatened or bribed.

Little is known about online abuse of children inside China. In 2025 the US CyberTipline, which collects reports from technology companies, received 9,406 reports for China and 1,933,900 for India, because most US platforms are blocked in China.

The adoption programme has ended. The 2025 US reports say traffickers still take girls from Pakistan, Vietnam and Laos to China as brides, and that displaced girls in Myanmar remain at risk. The international records show almost nothing about online abuse of children inside China.

DEU.story:
In January 1980 the Archdiocese of Munich, then led by Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, accepted Fr Peter Hullermann from the Diocese of Essen for therapy after Essen had suspended him over the abuse of a boy. Munich gave him parish work, and he abused minors again. He was convicted in 1986, given a suspended sentence, and kept serving in Bavarian parishes until 2010. Later university studies of dioceses found such transfers common. In Münster, historians found in 2022 that at least 610 minors had been abused by 196 clerics since 1945, estimated the real number of victims at eight to ten times higher, and found that bishops usually transferred accused priests.

Youth offices, the public agencies responsible for children in care, also placed children with abusers. From the late 1960s Berlin's youth authorities, on the advice of the psychologist Helmut Kentler, placed boys in foster care with men known to be paedophiles, a practice that continued into the 2000s. In Lügde, a youth office placed a foster daughter with Andreas V., who lived at a campsite. Police received two tips about him in 2016 and did not act. In 2019 he and a second man were convicted of abusing 32 children there between 1998 and 2018, and a state parliamentary inquiry found they could have been stopped two years earlier.

The legal deadlines for bringing cases, called statutes of limitations, also protected offenders. At the Odenwaldschule, a boarding school, former pupils came forward in 1998, and prosecutors dropped the case because the deadline had passed. In 2013 the Bundestag, the federal parliament, extended the deadline for civil claims from 3 to 30 years, but not for claims that had already expired.

Abuse material is also hosted and traded from Germany. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity, acted on 18,401 internet addresses of abuse material on German servers. In 2021 German police took down Boystown, a platform run by German administrators that had 400,000 registered users.

Church and state inquiries have now counted many victims of abuse in German institutions, and many older cases can no longer be taken to court.

FIN.story:
In 2011 the Central Committee of Conservative Laestadian Congregations (SRK), the largest revivalist movement within Finland's Lutheran church, with about 35,000 members, announced that an internal report had found 70 to 100 cases of child sexual abuse within the movement since the 1980s. Most of the abuse took place inside members' families. The SRK admitted that its officials had mishandled the cases, had not used expert help and had lacked the knowledge to respond. A study of abuse in the movement by Johanna Hurtig of the University of Tampere was published the same year.

The state's own record was examined later. A study by the Ministry of Social Affairs and Health interviewed about 300 people who had been placed by child welfare services in institutions or foster families between 1937 and 1983, and found maltreatment and violence in every form of care. On 20 November 2016 the Finnish government made an official apology to them.

What is known in Finland comes from one ministry study and one religious movement's report on itself. The ministry study did not count how many children in state care were sexually abused, and the only figures for the SRK come from the movement.

GTM.story:
In 1977, during Guatemala's internal armed conflict, a decree allowed notaries, private lawyers who certify documents, to complete adoptions without a judge's approval. A 2009 study by the Peace Archives, a government office, reviewed 333 adoption files from 1977 to 1989 and found that the army and the National Police brought children into the adoption system, and that courts declared children abandoned with little effort to find their parents.

After the war ended in 1996, adoptions abroad rose every year. Private notaries handled about 98 percent of them, acting for both sides without court review, and charged $35,000 or more per child. In the 2007 financial year the United States issued 4,728 visas to children adopted from Guatemala. In August 2007 police found 46 children, most without proper documents, at Casa Quivira, a private adoption home in Antigua. In December 2007 Guatemala passed a law meeting the Hague Convention, the international treaty on adoption, and from 1 January 2008 it stopped new adoptions to the United States. In 2010 CICIG, an international commission investigating crime in Guatemala, studied 153 adoptions and found that 78 percent had broken the law in some way.

The Hogar Seguro Virgen de la Asunción, a state children's home built for 500, held about 700. Girls there alleged sexual abuse by staff, prosecutors had recommended closing it, and in November 2016 the Human Rights Ombudsman reported a trafficking network recruiting children from the home. On 7 March 2017, after an escape, police locked a group of girls in a room. The next day one girl set a mattress on fire, and 41 girls died. In August 2025 a judge convicted six former officials, including the former social welfare secretary, Carlos Rodas, who received 25 years, and said the fire followed reported abuses that no one had acted on.

The notary trade ended with the 2008 halt on new adoptions to the United States. The 2025 US State Department report says gangs and other criminal groups exploit girls in Guatemalan cities, and Guatemalan children are trafficked into Mexico and the United States.

IRL.story:
From the 1930s to the 1990s the Irish state funded industrial schools, residential institutions for children taken into care, and Catholic religious orders ran them. The Ryan Commission, a state inquiry, reported in 2009 that more than 30,000 children had passed through over 250 church-run institutions, that sexual abuse was endemic in the boys' institutions run mainly by the Christian Brothers, and that state inspections had failed. Because the Christian Brothers sued, its report named no abusers.

Bishops dealt with complaints against priests inside the church. In 1975 Seán Brady, later a cardinal, attended meetings where two teenage victims of Fr Brendan Smyth were sworn to secrecy, and their evidence never reached the police. His order, the Norbertines, moved him between parishes and countries, including the United States, and he abused at least 143 children. In 1994 the Irish government's delay over a request to extradite him to Northern Ireland led to its collapse. The Murphy Report of 2009 found that four archbishops of Dublin had not told the Gardaí, Ireland's police, what they knew. In Cloyne, an inquiry found in 2011 that nine complaints made after the church adopted reporting rules in 1996 were not passed on to the Gardaí.

A separate commission reported in 2021 that about 9,000 children had died between 1922 and 1998 in the 14 mother and baby homes, where unmarried women gave birth, and 4 county homes it examined, and that several were linked to illegal adoptions, many to the United States. In 2018 the government found that the St Patrick's Guild adoption society had falsely registered 126 adopted people as their adoptive parents' birth children, and a 2021 review estimated that between 5,540 and 19,980 adoption files might show similar signs.

In 2024 a scoping inquiry recorded 2,395 allegations of sexual abuse against 884 people at 308 schools run by religious orders, and the government announced a full investigation. More than half of them are dead. The 2021 adoption review did not recommend checking every file, so the number of people living under falsified birth records is not known.

KEN.story:
In December 2006 UNICEF and Kenya's Ministry of Home Affairs published a joint study of four beach resort areas. It found that up to 30 percent of girls aged 12 to 18 living there were involved in casual sex work, and that two to three thousand children were in full-time commercial sex. Kenyans made up 38 percent of the buyers, and tourists from Italy, Germany and Switzerland 44 percent. Vice President Moody Awori accepted the findings and said the police and local communities had failed to enforce the law.

The trade continued and moved. The 2025 US State Department trafficking report cites a 2023 study by a non-governmental organisation estimating that more than 2,000 children were sold for sex in Kilifi and Kwale counties, and says the abuse there is moving from hotels into private villas and holiday homes. The report also describes rings bringing underage girls from Uganda's Karamoja region to Nairobi, and notes concerns that officials take part, with no action reported against any of them.

Babies and young children were also bought and sold in Nairobi. In 2020 a year-long BBC investigation found children taken from homeless mothers in Nairobi and sold for about £350 to £550, A clinical social worker at Mama Lucy Kibaki Hospital, a government hospital, sold an abandoned two-week-old boy to undercover reporters for 300,000 shillings. The BBC said he appeared to keep his job.

Children were also abused in homes funded from abroad. At Nyumbani, a Nairobi home for children with HIV that drew large donations from the United States, a 2021 investigation by USAID, the US government's aid agency, found claims credible that volunteers, caregivers and other children had raped children there. A USAID memo said the co-founder had known of abuse allegations since 2006 and had failed to respond. The co-founder stepped down in 2023 after questions from the Washington Post.

Since the 2006 study no Kenyan government inquiry appears in the records gathered for this map, and what is known has come from foreign governments, charities and journalists. The most recent describe children still sold for sex on the coast.

LVA.story:
In September 1999 Latvian television reported on Logos Centrs, an agency in Riga run by Jurijs Jurjevs that presented itself as a modelling agency. Prosecutors investigated and charged seven people with running a ring that sold children for sex and filmed their abuse. According to Latvian press reports, 67 people, 61 of them minors, were sexually exploited, and the agency had catalogued about 3,000 minors. Andris Meinarts, a customer, was convicted on 21 counts of sexually abusing minors and given ten years, the maximum sentence, and Jurjevs received more than four years.

The case then became a political one. The Saeima, Latvia's parliament, set up an investigation commission chaired by the opposition MP Jānis Ādamsons. In February 2000 Ādamsons publicly linked the former prime minister Andris Šķēle, the former justice minister Valdis Birkavs and the head of the State Revenue Service, Andrejs Sončiks, to the case. In August 2000 the Prosecutor General's Office closed the cases against them and said it was "fully proved" that the information given to the commission about them was false. None of the three was charged. Ādamsons was later convicted of slander, and in 2007 the Supreme Court upheld a fine of 10,400 lats.

Latvia also sent children abroad for adoption. A Latvian law preventing adoptions to the United States took effect on 1 July 2022.

The agency's operators and at least one customer were convicted, and the claims against senior politicians were disproved. No later national inquiry into the sexual exploitation of children in Latvia appears in the records gathered for this map.

NOR.story:
In 2004 a Norwegian government report, NOU 2004:23, examined municipal children's homes and state special schools between 1945 and 1980 and found neglect and abuse there, some of it serious and including sexual abuse. In 2005 a committee of the Storting, Norway's parliament, recommended that the state's compensation scheme pay up to NOK 300,000 and require a lower burden of proof.

Norway also took in children from abroad. Between 1955 and 2008 it received 6,295 children from South Korea, and in 1974 and 1975, when South Korea tried to stop sending children, Scandinavian diplomats pressed it to continue. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found that Korean agencies had sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand and had falsely registered children with known parents as orphans.

In 2023 Norway appointed a committee to investigate the adoptions. Its report, NOU 2026:7, presented in June 2026, examined adoptions from 12 countries since the 1950s and found illegal or unethical practices and clear failings in the Norwegian system throughout the period. It recorded a kidnapped child adopted to Norway, a mother told she would get money if she consented, and deliberately falsified documents. Payments to orphanages were sometimes linked to the number of children adopted. Norwegian adoption organisations did not always tell the authorities about payments or errors, and the authorities kept approving adoptions after learning of the risks.

In 2026, using a payment-tracing method developed the year before, Norwegian police helped police in seven countries arrest 28 men suspected of paying cryptocurrency for access to hidden online forums with abuse videos. After the US release of Jeffrey Epstein documents, the former prime minister Thorbjørn Jagland was charged in February 2026 with aggravated corruption over gifts, travel and loans. The case concerns corruption, not abuse, and he denies the charges.

Adopted people in Norway now have an official finding that the system that brought many of them there broke the law at times. In 2025 one Korean-born adoptee gave notice of a lawsuit against the state alleging that her adoption was illegal.

POL.story:
Between 1940 and 1945 Nazi Germany took children it judged "racially valuable" from occupied Poland and placed them with German families under new identities. DW reports estimates of up to 200,000. In 1948 a US military tribunal at Nuremberg convicted 13 officials of the SS race office and the Lebensborn homes of crimes that included kidnapping these children.

In March 2019 the Polish Episcopal Conference, the national body of Catholic bishops, reported that 382 priests had been accused of abusing 625 children between 1990 and mid-2018. Documentaries by the Sekielski brothers in 2019 and 2020 led the Vatican to investigate Polish bishops, and in 2020 Pope Francis accepted the resignation of Bishop Edward Janiak, accused of failing to act against a priest.

After a 2020 documentary on abuse and alleged cover-ups in the church, the government set up a State Commission on Paedophilia. Its 2021 report studied 345 cases involving 188 girls and 173 boys. Relatives made up 35 percent of the abusers and clergy almost 30 percent, and in half the cases no one had noticed signs of abuse. The commission sent 137 notifications to prosecutors and recommended ending the statute of limitations, the legal deadline for bringing a case, for child sexual abuse. In 2026 a commission in the Diocese of Sosnowiec found at least 50 children harmed since 1992, and that bishops had often been warned and had moved accused priests to other parishes.

Polish clergy were also accused of abusing children abroad. Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, the Vatican's ambassador to the Dominican Republic, was recalled to the Vatican in 2013 while Dominican authorities investigated him, and the Vatican later told Polish prosecutors its law did not allow his extradition. He died before trial. Fr Wojciech Gil, who had also worked there, returned to Poland, which has no extradition treaty with the Dominican Republic. Polish police arrested him, and in 2015 a court sentenced him to seven years.

Church and state counts have both found clergy among the largest groups of people who abused children in Poland. The number of victims beyond the cases studied is not known.

SVK.story:
In March 2024 the Slovak Catholic bishops' commission for the protection of minors published its first evaluation report on sexual abuse in the church, covering complaints made from 1990 to 2023. It counted 68 complaints, of which 50 concerned the Latin-rite dioceses, 3 the Greek Catholic eparchies, which are the dioceses of the Eastern-rite church, and 15 the religious orders. The commission confirmed 39 of them, involving more than 44 victims. It could not confirm 5, could not resolve 7, and 17 were still open.

This is the only national count of abuse in institutions in Slovakia found for this map, and it was made by the church about itself. No state inquiry or survey of the general population has been found, so the figures show only the complaints that reached the church.

TTO.story:
In 1997 the Cabinet of Trinidad and Tobago appointed a task force chaired by Robert Sabga to examine the country's children's homes. It visited nine homes. At St Dominic's Children's Home it found that a male employee had repeatedly sexually abused some 30 to 40 children. When this was discovered he was asked to resign, and he was allegedly helped to find work at a hospital. The task force also recorded beatings at St Jude's School for Girls.

The government never published the report. Its findings became public only in May 2022, when the Trinidad Express newspaper reported them, 25 years after the task force was set up.

The 2025 US State Department trafficking report says that most victims of sex trafficking in the country are women and girls from Venezuela, Colombia, the Dominican Republic and Guyana, and that non-governmental organisations allege officials help traffickers move them and bring them into the country.

What happened to the St Dominic's employee after the task force reported, and whether the homes were changed, is not recorded, and no later inquiry into the country's children's homes appears in the records gathered for this map.

ZAF.story:
In 1979 Fettes College, a school in Edinburgh, dismissed the teacher Iain Wares but gave him a glowing reference. He went on to teach in South Africa, where he later abused children; South Africa approved his extradition to Scotland, which he was still contesting in 2025. Fr Georg Kerkhoff, a German priest with abuse cases pending at home, worked in South Africa and was tried there for abusing boys at a 2008 camp before being extradited and jailed in Germany in 2015.

The British barrister John Smyth moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, after a 1982 internal report of the Iwerne Trust, the evangelical charity he had chaired, described how he beat boys he met at its camps. Refused re-entry to Zimbabwe, he moved to South Africa in 2001. The Makin Review, published in England in 2024, found it highly likely that he kept abusing until his death in Cape Town in 2018. He was never charged anywhere.

In June 2026 the South African Human Rights Commission described sexual violence in schools as systemic. It recorded 826 complaints of sexual misconduct made between 2021 and 2025 to the South African Council for Educators, the body that registers teachers. It found that a teacher struck off by the council is not automatically added to the register of people barred from working with children, and that 10,748 convicted offenders had not been entered on the National Register for Sex Offenders.

The 2025 US State Department trafficking report says traffickers recruit children from rural areas and sell them for sex in Gauteng and Western Cape, that brothel owners use drugs to control them, that some parents sell their own children, and that low-level corruption and complicity among officials continued.

In the case of Timothy Omotoso, first reported in 2017, mistrial motions and recusals delayed the trial for eight years, and a whistleblower, Pamela Mabini, was shot dead in March 2025, weeks before the verdict.

Because of the gaps the commission found, teachers removed for sexual misconduct and convicted sex offenders may be missing from the registers meant to keep them away from South African children.
